column2: Boot (strapping) pins are read by the chip at power-up to decide how to boot. On the ESP32: GPIO 0, 2, 5, 12, 15. If GPIO 12 is pulled HIGH at boot, the chip uses the wrong flash voltage and the board fails to boot. Avoid attaching anything that pulls these pins at power-up.
Input-only pins: on the ESP32, GPIO 34-39 can only be inputs and have no internal pull-up.
Pins used by the flash: on many ESP32 boards, GPIO 6-11 are connected to the flash chip and must not be used.
UART pins for uploading: TX0/RX0 are used for uploading and the Serial Monitor. Attaching a module there can make uploads fail.
A button on an input pin with no resistor and no INPUT_PULLUP. What happens when the button is not pressed?
The pin floats and reads HIGH/LOW at random.
A 5 V sensor outputs a 5 V digital signal. Can it go straight to an ESP32 pin?
No. Lower it first with a voltage divider (for example 1 kΩ and 2 kΩ) or a level shifter.
The 12-bit ESP32 ADC reads 2048. Roughly what is the voltage if the upper limit is 3.1 V?
About 2048 / 4095 × 3.1 ≈ 1.55 V. Only roughly, because the ESP32 ADC is not fully linear.
Buttons and reading pins
PWM, servos and motors
How a microcontroller sets brightness, speed and position.

PWM switches a signal on and off very fast. The duty cycle is the percentage of time it is on. An LED looks dimmer because the eye averages its flicker; a motor turns slower because it feels the average. The microcontroller pin only supplies the PWM signal; a big load is switched through a MOSFET or motor driver.
A 50% duty on 5 V feels like about 2.5 V to the load.

A servo does not read the average, but the pulse width repeated 50 times per second. Inside the servo is a potentiometer that reads the arm's position, and the servo keeps correcting until the position matches the command. If it is commanded to an angle it cannot reach (the arm hits the frame), the servo keeps pushing: vibrating, humming and drawing a large current.
The wider the pulse, the larger the angle.
Servo power from a separate source (5-6 V), not the board's 3V3 pin. A small servo such as the SG90 can draw hundreds of mA when moving or held.
The servo GND and board GND are joined (Chapter 2), and the board pin goes only to the signal wire (orange or yellow).
DC motors and steppers

A DC motor turns both ways with an H-bridge (motor driver): four electronic switches that reverse the current direction. Direction from two pins, speed from PWM. Swapping the two motor wires reverses its direction.
A DC motor draws the most current when it starts turning and when it is stalled, several times its normal current. Choose a driver and source that can handle that current.
A stepper moves step by step and needs a dedicated driver (A4988, DRV8825, ULN2003 for the 28BYJ-48).

A servo is commanded to 180° and then keeps making small movements at the end, humming, and the power module's light flickers. That servo cannot reach 180° because of its frame, and keeps trying. The fix is an angle limit it can reach without vibration, not more power.
25% duty on 5 V. Roughly what does the motor feel?
About 1.25 V on average. A small motor may only hum without turning.
A servo sits quietly at 90° but vibrates constantly at 180°. What does it mean?
At 180° the arm hits a mechanical limit, and the servo keeps trying to reach that angle. Reduce the angle limit in the code.
One robot wheel spins the opposite way from what is expected. Two ways to fix it?
Swap that motor's two wires at the driver, or reverse the direction in the code.

Communication and reading module specifications
How the board talks to sensors and modules, and what to check before connecting.
What to remember
UART (Serial)
one device's TX to the other's RX (crossed); the speed (baud rate) on both sides must match
SDA, SCL, GND
many devices on two wires, told apart by address; needs pull-ups; short wires (tens of cm)
SCK, MOSI, MISO, CS
fast; three wires shared, each device has its own CS pin
DATA, GND (and VCC)
DS18B20 and similar; needs a pull-up of about 4.7 kΩ on DATA
Dedicated single-wire signals
DHT11/DHT22 use their own protocol; the module usually already carries a pull-up
one ADC pin
the voltage directly represents the value; sensitive to noise and long wires
All I2C devices share SDA and SCL. Two devices with the same address cannot be on the same bus without changing an address.
Reading a module's specification before connecting
Operating voltage (VCC): 3.3 V only, 5 V only, or 3.3-5 V? A 5 V module given 3.3 V often works half-way; a 3.3 V module given 5 V can be destroyed.
Signal logic level: a module given 5 V usually outputs 5 V signals too. For a 3.3 V board, check whether the module has a level shifter.
Current: how much it draws when active and when idle. This decides the power source and battery life.
Interface and address: what the I2C address is, which CS pin SPI needs, what the default UART baud rate is.
Pin names: read the labels on the board, do not guess from position. Similar modules from different sellers can have a different pin order.

An I2C OLED display is not detected by the I2C scanner program. The most frequent causes, in order: SDA and SCL swapped, VCC or GND not connected, the I2C pins in the code differ from the pins used, and the wrong address in the code (0x3C and 0x3D are both common). On UART, strange characters in the Serial Monitor almost always mean a different baud rate.
Two boards are connected over UART but no data arrives. What are the first two things to check?
TX to RX crossed (not TX to TX), and the GND of both boards connected. Then the same baud rate.
You connect two identical I2C sensors. What is the problem?
The same address. Many sensors have a pin or jumper to select a second address; if not, you need an I2C multiplexer or a second I2C bus.
A DS18B20 temperature sensor always reads −127 or 85. Which component is often forgotten?
A 4.7 kΩ pull-up resistor from DATA to VCC.

Multimeter and measuring tools
The most important tool for building. Most misreadings come from the dial and the sockets.
The dial chooses what is measured, the socket sets the red probe's path.
batteries, regulators, board pins
circuit on, probes on two points
household power
not used in low-voltage projects
resistors, wires, resistive sensors
power OFF, preferably remove the component
Beep (continuity)
whether two points are connected
power OFF
LEDs, diodes, polarity
circuit opened, multimeter inserted in series; the red probe moves to another socket
COM is always for the black probe. VΩmA is for almost every measurement. 10A is only for measuring large currents in series.
A minus number means the probes are reversed. The magnitude is still correct.
"OL" or "1" at the left of the display means out of range or not connected.
Manual-range multimeter (with 2, 20, 200 on the dial): choose a range above the number you expect, for example 20 V for a 7.4 V battery.
Ω mode on a component that is still installed also measures the other components connected to it, so the result can mislead.
After measuring current, put the red probe back in the VΩ socket. Forgetting this step is the most common way to blow a multimeter's fuse.
In A mode or the 10A socket, the multimeter has almost no resistance. Touching it to the two battery terminals is the same as a short circuit: the multimeter's fuse blows, or worse.
Other measuring tools
A cheap logic analyzer (the 8-channel version is easy to find) shows I2C, SPI and UART digital signals on a laptop: very helpful when a module "will not talk".
An oscilloscope shows the shape of voltage over time: noise, PWM, and momentary voltage dips (brownouts) that a multimeter does not catch.
A USB meter shows the voltage and current from a USB port: an easy way to measure a board's consumption.
When measuring a battery, the display stays at 0 even with the switch ON and OFF. It turns out the dial points to 10 A, not V⎓. After turning it to V⎓, the switch ON reads 7.8 V and OFF 0 V.
Why must the multimeter not be touched to a battery while the red probe is in the 10A socket?
Current mode has almost no resistance, so a short circuit happens through the multimeter.
The display shows −3.3 V. What does it mean?
The red and black probes are reversed. The voltage is still 3.3 V.
Why must the beep test be done with power off?
The beep test pushes a small current from the multimeter's own battery. Voltage from the circuit can make the result wrong or damage the multimeter.
Know your multimeter
Breadboards, connectors and soldering
Many "electronics" problems turn out to be connections that are not tight enough.
Five holes in one column are connected; the center gap separates the two sides; the power rails are connected along the row.
The center gap is made for ICs and modules with two rows of legs, so the left and right legs are not connected.
The power rails on a long board are sometimes broken in the middle (see the broken red-blue line). Measure with the beep test if in doubt.
An ESP32 DevKit board is often too wide for one breadboard: it covers all the holes on one side. Use two breadboards side by side or an expansion board.
A breadboard is not suited to large currents (above about 1 A) and its contacts can wear out. For motor lines, use screw terminals or connectors.
Used for

come loose easily; thin wire; can break inside

make sure it is not reversed; check the red-black order, which differs between sellers

A good solder joint wraps the leg and the pad; a cold joint only sits on top.

Heat the thing being soldered, not the solder. Touch the iron tip to the leg and pad together for 1-2 seconds, touch the solder to the joint until it flows, lift away, then do not move it until it sets.
Wires: strip, twist the strands, coat thinly with solder first (tinning), then join.
Slide the heat shrink on before soldering, because it cannot be added after both ends are connected.
Give every joint a gentle tug when done. A joint that comes off with a gentle tug will certainly come off in use.

Two causes are often confused. A loose connection: touching it presses the contact until it connects or breaks. A floating point: GND or an input is not connected, and your hand conducts noise. Tell them apart with the beep test (Chapter 2) and by pressing with a non-conductive object such as a toothpick.
An LED on a breadboard does not light. The LED leg and the resistor are in column 10, rows a and f. What is wrong?
Row a is on the upper side of the gap, f on the lower side: not connected. Move them to the same side (a-e).
The solder joint is a dull ball and the wire wobbles a little. What needs to be done?
That is a cold joint. Reheat until the solder flows around the leg and pad, adding a little fresh solder if needed.

How to find faults
A way of working that finds problems in minutes, not hours.
Write down the symptom exactly. "The sensor reads 0 constantly since it was moved to battery" is more useful than "the sensor is broken".
Measure, do not guess. Measure the voltage at the point of use (the module's VCC pin), not only at the source.
Isolate. Remove all the modules, power on, then add them one at a time until the problem appears.
Swap with a known good one. Move the module to another pin or another board; replace the jumper wire.
Change one thing at a time. Replacing the capacitor, code and wire all at once leaves you not knowing which was the cause.
The check order that is most often right: power → shared GND → polarity → connections → pins and code → mechanical.
Common causes
Board does not show up on the USB port
the USB cable is charge-only, the CH340/CP210x driver is not installed
try another data cable; install the driver
ESP32 upload fails with "Failed to connect"
the chip does not enter upload mode, or a module is on the boot/TX0/RX0 pins
hold the BOOT button when the upload starts; remove modules from those pins
Random restarts, "Brownout detector was triggered"
momentary power dips (WiFi, motor, servo)
better USB cable, stronger source, capacitor, big loads on a separate source
Bootloop with a flash error message at power-up
unstable power during boot, or a boot pin pulled
remove all modules, check GPIO 12, erase the flash and upload again
I2C sensor not found
SDA/SCL swapped, wrong address, wrong VCC, different pins in the code
run the I2C scanner, check the wires one by one
Sensor numbers random or changing when touched
floating input or lost shared GND
beep-test the GND; make sure there is a pull-up
Relay does not click
active-LOW module, a 3.3 V signal too weak for a 5 V module, not enough coil power
invert the logic; measure the module's VCC; try a signal from a transistor
LED does not light
reversed, resistor too large, wrong breadboard column
check the long leg; measure the voltage at the LED
Strange characters in the Serial Monitor
different baud rate
make the number in Serial.begin match the Serial Monitor
Compile fails: unknown function (for example ledcAttach)
the board core version differs from the code example
update the board core in Boards Manager, or use the example for your version
Module or regulator hot
voltage too high, short circuit, linear regulator with a large difference
switch off the power, measure the input voltage, check the wiring
You replace the capacitor, code and wire all at once, and the problem goes away. What is the drawback?
You do not know which was the cause, and the same problem can return without you knowing where to look.
A project works while USB is connected but not on battery. What do you measure first?
The voltage at the board's and modules' power pins while on battery, especially when WiFi or loads are active. Then the shared GND between the battery and the modules.
Make your own notes
Low voltage is safe if treated correctly. Household power is not.

220 V household power can kill. Do not connect relays, modules or wires to household power until you really understand insulation, closed enclosures, fuses and the safe spacing between conductors. To control a lamp or appliance, a smart plug or certified module is far safer.

Li-ion and LiPo batteries: a short circuit can heat the wires in seconds and set the cell on fire. Fit a fuse near the battery for high-current projects, and always use protection (a BMS or a module with protection).

Charge under supervision, on a surface that does not burn easily, with a charger that suits the battery type. Do not charge a cell that is swollen, dented, leaking, or that has sat very empty for a long time.
Store batteries about half full for long storage, and remove them from the circuit.
Disconnect power before soldering or moving wires.
Regulators, power resistors and motors can get hot. Touch with the back of a finger first.
Large electrolytic capacitors still hold charge briefly after power is off. At low voltage this is not dangerous to the body, but it can spark if the legs are shorted.
Solder and solder wire: work in a ventilated room, and wash your hands afterwards.
